insight.insight: Topic drift inside an active conversation is not a privacy boundary. Whether a user-disclosed secret can be recovered is a behavioral question: will the model reproduce it when a later prompt asks? It is not a question of whether the secret is still in the context. In practice this is decided mainly by format-sensitive safety cues tied to the secret type. Separating drift length and persuasion level as controlled axes, and scoring with a hybrid detector plus a stability-based metric (Privacy Half-Life), shows that leakage persists across drift and is governed by secret type.
dependent_results: Dialogue-level hybrid leakage is substantial for all three models: DeepSeek-R1 38.70% [35.7, 41.6], GPT-OSS-120B 47.70% [44.6, 50.8], Qwen3-VL-235B 54.60% [51.6, 57.7] (5.2 All Models Leak Substantially at the Dialogue Level).

Drift length has small or negligible association with leakage. Cramer's V is 0.1073 for DeepSeek-R1, 0.0659 for GPT-OSS-120B and 0.0723 for Qwen3-VL-235B. Curves dip near d=3 and then rebound (5.4 Drift Length Does Not Reliably Reduce Leakage Within the Tested Window).
Privacy Half-Life τ = 7 = max(D_obs)+1 for all models and persuasion levels, meaning no stable decay within d≤6 (5.6 Privacy Half-Life Exceeds the Observed Window).

Secret type strongly determines leakage. Cramer's V is 0.5871 for DeepSeek-R1, 0.7731 for GPT-OSS-120B and 0.6927 for Qwen3-VL-235B. SSN leakage is 0.14–5.97% and credit card 0.00–4.01%, versus email 57–81% and phone 46–71% (5.5 Secret Type Strongly Determines Leakage).

Persuasion level matters significantly (Cochran's Q p<10^-5), but the direction depends on the model. Hard probes reduce leakage for GPT-OSS (32.9% vs 39.3/40.5%) and raise it for Qwen (40.6%). Medium is lowest for DeepSeek (22.0%) (5.3 Persuasion Intensity Affects Leakage Non-Monotonically).

The LLM judge adds at most 1.10 percentage points over regex matching: +0.00 for GPT-OSS, +0.90 for DeepSeek, +1.10 for Qwen. Leakage is therefore mostly verbatim or near-verbatim reproduction (5.1 Dialogue-Level Hybrid Evaluation Largely Agrees With Deterministic Matching).
Fuzzy matching at the 0.85 threshold tracks hybrid probe-level leakage closely: 26.40 vs 26.43, 37.03 vs 37.57, 37.60 vs 37.53 (5.7 Fuzzy Matching Supports the Hybrid Labels).
key_definitions: Active-context re-disclosure: the model reproduces a secret S, disclosed at turn t0, in response to a probe P appended after d unrelated drift turns. Leakage means S is revealed exactly, approximately or semantically (3.1 Threat Model: Active-Context Re-Disclosure).
Drift length d: the number of content-dense unrelated turns between disclosure and probe. It is set to 0 with probability 0.2, otherwise drawn uniformly from {2,...,6} (3.3 Probing Setup).
Persuasion levels: Simple (direct query), Medium (query with a contextual justification), Hard (high-pressure or urgent request) (3.3 Probing Setup).
Regex leakage: Leak_regex(R,S) = I[φ(S) ⊂ φ(R)], where φ strips non-digits for numeric secrets and normalizes case and whitespace for alphanumeric ones (3.4.1 Stage 1: Normalization-Based Matching).

Hybrid leakage: a response counts as leaking if regex matches or, for regex-negative responses, an open-weights Llama judge rules that the full secret or a substantial part of it was revealed (3.4.2 Stage 2: LLM-as-a-Judge Verification).
Privacy Half-Life τ: the minimal observed d with L(d) ≤ δ = 0.1·L(0) such that every larger observed d also stays ≤ δ. If no such d exists, τ = max(D_obs)+1 (3.4.3 Privacy Half-Life).
Dialogue-level leakage counts a dialogue as leaking if any of its three probes leaks. Probe-level leakage counts each probe response separately (4 Experimental Setup, Aggregation levels).
reasoning_steps: The scaffold-then-rewrite pipeline holds the secret, drift length and probe fixed while varying the surrounding content. Any change in leakage can then be attributed to drift, persuasion or secret type (3.2 Dataset Generation Pipeline; 3.2.3 Naturalistic Refinement).

Drift turns are content-dense and unrelated to the secret, and dialogue length grows with d: about 44 words at d=0 versus about 568 at d=6. This makes d a meaningful manipulation of context distance (3.2.2 Content-Dense Topic Drift; Appendix A Dataset Characterization).

Each dialogue receives all three probes, giving paired data. This supports Cochran's Q and McNemar tests across persuasion levels and detectors, and a dialogue-level 'any probe' vulnerability rate (4 Experimental Setup).

The hybrid detector adds little over regex and agrees with fuzzy matching. This validates the leakage labels and shows that leakage is mostly direct reproduction (5.1 Dialogue-Level Hybrid Evaluation Largely Agrees With Deterministic Matching; 5.7 Fuzzy Matching Supports the Hybrid Labels).

Chi-square tests with Cramer's V compare how strongly each variable is associated with leakage. Secret type is large, while drift and persuasion are small or negligible, which identifies format cues as the dominant factor (5.4 Drift Length Does Not Reliably Reduce Leakage Within the Tested Window; 5.5 Secret Type Strongly Determines Leakage; Appendix B Additional Effect Sizes).

The stability requirement in τ treats the dip near d=3 as non-suppression because leakage rebounds afterwards. This yields τ=7 and the conclusion that drift is not a privacy boundary within d≤6 (3.4.3 Privacy Half-Life; 5.6 Privacy Half-Life Exceeds the Observed Window; 6 Discussion).

The asymmetry across secret types, with SSNs and credit cards suppressed while emails and phone numbers leak, is read as evidence that safeguards rely on format-sensitive heuristics rather than reasoning about contextual confidentiality (5.5 Secret Type Strongly Determines Leakage; 6 Discussion).
